title: THE SIN JESUS SAID WILL NEVER BE FORGIVEN: WHAT IF YOU’VE ALREADY COMMITTED IT?
paragraphs: THE SIN JESUS SAID WILL NEVER BE FORGIVEN: WHAT IF YOU’VE ALREADY COMMITTED IT?

What Does It Really Mean to Blaspheme Against the Holy Spirit… and Can a Christian Commit That Sin? A disturbing accusation, a terrifying warning, and the extraordinary mercy of Jesus Christ. — Matthew 12:22–32
There is a kind of fear that doesn't let you sleep.
It doesn't always announce itself with tears. Sometimes it arrives quietly, when the house is dark, when everyone else is resting, and your mind suddenly remembers something you said years ago.
Something terrible.
Something you wish you could take back.

Maybe you were angry at God. Maybe you mocked something holy. Maybe you had a season when you wanted nothing to do with Christianity. Maybe you deliberately sinned after knowing what Scripture says. Or perhaps an ugly, blasphemous thought entered your mind, and you were so horrified by it that you wondered whether it revealed something unforgivable inside you.
And then you remembered the words of Jesus.
“But the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.” — Matthew 12:31, KJV
Suddenly, every other promise about forgiveness seemed to grow quiet.
What if that verse is about me?
What if I crossed a line I cannot uncross?
What if I am praying to a God who has already decided never to forgive me?
And perhaps the most painful question of all:
What if I still believe in Jesus, still want Him, still desperately need His mercy… but it is already too late?
If those questions have ever haunted you, please stay with me.
Because the answer cannot be found by isolating one frightening sentence from the mouth of Jesus. We have to return to the actual moment He spoke it.
We have to see the suffering man standing before Him.
We have to hear the accusation that came from religious leaders who should have recognized the work of God.
And we have to understand why Jesus gave one of the most severe warnings recorded in the Gospels.
Because the same passage that contains a terrifying warning also reveals something extraordinary about the Savior who gave it.
But first, there is a detail in this story that many frightened Christians overlook.
Jesus did not begin this encounter by condemning a struggling sinner. He began by setting a captive man free.
Matthew 12:22 tells us that a demon-oppressed man was brought to Jesus. The man was blind and unable to speak.
Imagine his world.

He could not see the faces around him. He could not express what was happening inside him. The people who brought him to Jesus knew he needed help, but the passage does not tell us how long he had suffered or what his days had been like.
We should not invent details Scripture does not give us.
But we can understand something of the helplessness of a man who could neither see nor speak.
Then Jesus healed him.
Matthew records that the man could both speak and see.
The crowd was astonished.
People began asking whether Jesus could be the Son of David, the promised Messiah.
For one extraordinary moment, a suffering man's restoration became a public witness to the kingdom of God.
And that is when the religious leaders spoke.
Not with gratitude.
Not with worship.
Not even with honest curiosity.
They accused Jesus of casting out demons through Beelzebul, the ruler of demons.
Read that carefully.
A man had been delivered from demonic oppression, and the Pharisees attributed the work of Jesus to demonic power.
They were not merely criticizing His teaching style or questioning a religious custom.
They were making a profoundly serious accusation about the spiritual source of His ministry.
The Gospel of Mark makes the connection unmistakable.
After recording Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, Mark explains:
“Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit.” — Mark 3:30, KJV
Those words matter enormously.
They tell us why the warning was spoken.
The issue was not a frightened believer accidentally choosing the wrong words during prayer.
It was not someone experiencing an intrusive thought.
It was not an exhausted Christian asking difficult questions.
It was the shocking act of attributing the liberating work of God's Spirit through Jesus to the power of Satan.
And Jesus answered them with devastating clarity.
He explained that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. If Satan were casting out Satan, his kingdom would be working toward its own destruction.
Then Jesus said:
“But if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God is come unto you.” — Matthew 12:28, KJV
Here is the turning point.
Jesus was not merely defending His reputation.
He was revealing what the miracle meant.
The kingdom of God had broken into their midst.
The stronger One had come to confront the powers of darkness.
A captive had been set free.
And some of the very people who were supposed to lead others toward God were describing God's liberating work as the activity of the devil.
Now we begin to understand why Jesus' warning was so severe.
But to understand it more deeply, we need to examine the language of Scripture itself.
The Greek text of Matthew 12:31 includes these words:
ἡ δὲ τοῦ πνεύματος βλασφημία οὐκ ἀφεθήσεται
Transliterated:
hē de tou pneumatos blasphēmia ouk aphethēsetai
A faithful rendering is:
“But the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.”
The word blasphēmia refers to slander, abusive speech, or speech that dishonors or reviles.
The word pneumatos means “Spirit” in this context, referring to the Holy Spirit.
And ouk aphethēsetai means “will not be forgiven.”
Jesus' warning is real.
It is serious.
We must never soften it into something harmless simply because it makes us uncomfortable.
But neither should we expand it beyond what Scripture teaches and use it to terrify people whom Jesus is calling to Himself.
Biblical faithfulness requires us to take both the warning and its context seriously.
So what, exactly, is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit?
In the immediate setting of Matthew 12, it involves a grave rejection and slander of the Spirit's unmistakable work through Jesus, specifically by attributing that work to Satan.
Many Christian interpreters also understand the warning to point toward a deeper, settled hardness of heart: a willful and persistent rejection of the Spirit's testimony to Jesus Christ.
These understandings are closely related, although Christians have differed over how broadly the sin should be defined and whether its precise historical form can be repeated today.
We should be careful here.
Scripture does not give us permission to pronounce that a particular living person has committed this sin.
Nor does it give us permission to declare that every moment of spiritual rebellion is automatically the unforgivable sin.
The warning concerns a profound rejection of the Spirit's witness to Christ, not every sinful thought or statement that passes through a human mind.
And this leads us to a question that may change how you understand your own spiritual struggle.
What is the difference between resisting God in weakness and hardening yourself against the very testimony that reveals Jesus as Savior?
Consider Peter.
Peter knew Jesus personally.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His miracles.
He had confessed Him as the Christ.
Yet on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
And the Gospel accounts tell us that Peter even denied Him with an oath and, on the third occasion, invoked a curse.
Imagine the shame that followed.
The man who had promised loyalty had publicly disowned his Lord.
Luke 22:61 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Then Peter remembered His words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Now imagine Peter waking the following morning with the memory of his own voice ringing in his ears.
I denied Him.
I said I did not know Him.
I failed the One I claimed to love.
Was Peter's sin serious?
Absolutely.
Was it spiritually devastating?
Yes.
But was Peter beyond the reach of Christ's mercy?
No.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21:15–19.
The same mouth that had denied Jesus would later proclaim Him publicly.
The same man who had collapsed under fear would become a bold witness to the risen Christ.
Peter's restoration does not mean denying Jesus is harmless.
It means that even grievous failure is not automatically the same thing as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
Peter's tears were not the end of his story because Peter's failure was not greater than his Savior's grace.
Now consider another man.
His name was Saul.
Before he became known as the apostle Paul, he persecuted the church.
He approved of violence against believers.
He sought to destroy the Christian movement.
And when Paul later described his former life, he used a startling word.
“Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.” — 1 Timothy 1:13, KJV
Did you notice?
Paul called himself a blasphemer.
And yet he obtained mercy.
That does not contradict Jesus' warning.
It demonstrates that not every form of blasphemy is identical to the particular sin Jesus warned about in Matthew 12.
Paul explicitly described his former actions as having been committed in ignorance and unbelief.
And Christ showed him mercy.
Think about that.
A persecutor became a preacher.
A man who tried to silence the church became a witness to the Gospel.
A man who once opposed the name of Jesus spent the rest of his life proclaiming that name.
And in 1 Timothy 1:15, Paul declared:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.”
If you are reading this with a history you are ashamed of, do not overlook what Paul's testimony teaches.
Your past rebellion is not proof that Christ cannot save you.
Your former unbelief is not proof that you are beyond forgiveness.
Your worst season does not automatically determine your eternal future.
But neither Peter's restoration nor Paul's conversion should make us careless about sin.
Grace is not permission to harden our hearts.
It is God's kindness calling us to repentance.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads us toward repentance.
And this is where the subject becomes deeply personal.
Because there are people who are not worried about blaspheming the Holy Spirit because they accidentally said something terrible.
They are worried because they have deliberately disobeyed God.
Again.
And again.
They have returned to sins they promised to abandon.
They have ignored convictions they once felt deeply.
They have allowed bitterness, lust, pride, dishonesty, resentment, or spiritual indifference to occupy places in their lives that should belong to Christ.
And now they wonder whether they have resisted God too many times.
Perhaps that is you.
Perhaps you know what it means to ask forgiveness at night and fall into the same temptation the following day.
Perhaps you have become exhausted by your own inconsistency.
You still believe the Bible.
You still believe Jesus died for sinners.
But you have begun to wonder whether those promises still apply to someone who knows better and keeps failing.
Listen carefully.
Repeated sin is dangerous. But repeated sin is not, by definition, the unforgivable sin described in Matthew 12.
The New Testament warns believers against hardening their hearts, grieving the Holy Spirit, and treating sin lightly.
Ephesians 4:30 says:
“And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.”
The Greek verb translated “grieve” is lypeite, from lypeō, meaning to cause sorrow or distress.
Paul was warning Christians that their conduct could grieve the Holy Spirit.
Notice whom he was addressing.
Believers.
People who belonged to the Christian community and were being instructed to put away sinful behavior.
If grieving the Holy Spirit automatically meant committing the unforgivable sin, Paul's instruction would lose its pastoral meaning.
He was calling them away from sinful conduct and toward the life appropriate to those redeemed in Christ.
Likewise, 1 Thessalonians 5:19 warns:
“Quench not the Spirit.”
These are serious commands.
They show that Christians can act contrary to the Spirit's work.
But Scripture does not teach that every instance of grieving or quenching the Spirit is the same as the blasphemy Jesus condemned in Matthew 12.
We must not confuse distinct biblical warnings.
And we must not turn every failure into a declaration of hopelessness.
Yet there is another danger.
Some people hear that explanation and immediately conclude that they have nothing to fear.
They reason that because they once prayed a salvation prayer, were baptized, attended church, or served in ministry, their present rebellion cannot matter.
But Jesus never taught that a religious history makes persistent unbelief harmless.
The warning in Matthew 12 should humble us.
Hebrews 3:13 warns about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Sin rarely announces its final destination when it first asks for your cooperation.
It often begins with a compromise you believe you can control.
A small dishonesty.
A secret habit.
A bitterness you refuse to surrender.
A conviction you repeatedly silence.
And over time, what once troubled your conscience may begin to feel normal.
That is one reason spiritual hardness is so dangerous.
Not because God's grace is weak.
But because a hardened heart increasingly refuses the very grace it needs.
The Holy Spirit testifies to Jesus Christ.
Jesus says in John 15:26 that the Spirit of truth will bear witness about Him.
In John 16:8, He explains that the Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.
And in John 16:14, Jesus says of the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me.”
That is crucial.
The Holy Spirit does not lead people away from the true Jesus.
He glorifies Christ.
He bears witness to Christ.
He exposes sin and directs people toward the truth revealed in Christ.
So when someone persistently and knowingly rejects that witness, the danger is not that they have discovered a sin stronger than Christ's sacrifice.
The danger is that they are rejecting the Savior to whom the Spirit points.
And there is no other Savior.
Acts 4:12 declares that salvation is found in no other name.
That is why this warning must never be treated casually.
But here is where we must address one of the most painful misunderstandings surrounding this passage.
If you are terrified that you committed the unforgivable sin, does that fear prove you have not committed it?
You may have heard someone say that if you are worried about it, you definitely have not done it.
That statement is often offered with compassionate intentions.
And there is an important pastoral insight behind it.
A person who genuinely desires Christ, grieves over sin, and longs for reconciliation is not displaying the same attitude as the Pharisees who defiantly attributed His liberating work to Satan.
That difference matters.
But fear alone is not an infallible spiritual test.

Some people experience intense religious anxiety, unwanted blasphemous thoughts, or recurring doubts about their salvation. Those experiences can be deeply distressing without indicating that they have committed the sin described in Matthew 12.
We should not tell someone to examine the intensity of their anxiety as though it could reveal God's final verdict.
The better question is not simply, “How afraid am I?”
It is:
“What does Scripture tell me to do with my sin, my fear, and my need for mercy?”
And the answer is not to keep searching your memory for an unforgivable sentence.
It is to turn toward Jesus Christ.
Listen to His own words.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Read that again.
Jesus did not say, “Whoever comes to Me with a respectable past.”
He did not say, “Whoever comes to Me without a history of terrible thoughts.”
He did not say, “Whoever comes to Me having never fallen into serious sin.”
He said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
The Greek expression behind “I will in no wise cast out” is:
οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω
ou mē ekbalō exō
The construction ou mē expresses emphatic negation.
In this promise, Jesus strongly assures those who come to Him that He will not cast them out.
That is not a promise we should weaken.
Nor should we use it to erase the warnings Jesus also gave.
Both belong to His teaching.
The same Savior who warned against blasphemy of the Spirit also promised to receive those who come to Him.
We do not honor Jesus by believing His warnings while doubting His promises.
And we do not honor Him by embracing His promises while dismissing His warnings.
We must hear both.
Perhaps this is the moment when someone needs to stop asking, “What if Jesus rejects me?” and begin listening to what Jesus actually says to those who come to Him.
Because salvation was never built upon your ability to maintain a flawless emotional state.
It rests upon the person and finished work of Jesus Christ.
He lived in obedience to the Father.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
His resurrection is not a decorative ending to a religious story.
It is the victory of the living Savior over death.
And the Gospel calls sinners to repent and believe in Him.
Not to earn forgiveness through endless self-punishment.
Not to prove themselves worthy by becoming emotionally exhausted.
Not to purchase peace through religious performance.
But to trust the crucified and risen Lord.
Consider 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Greek word translated “confess” is homologōmen, from homologeō, which carries the sense of acknowledging or confessing.
Confession is not pretending sin was insignificant.
It is agreeing with the truth about our sin before God.
And genuine repentance is not merely feeling frightened about consequences.
It involves turning from sin toward God.
But do not miss the foundation of forgiveness.
John says God is faithful and just.
Forgiveness is not God temporarily forgetting that He is holy.
It is inseparable from the saving work of Jesus Christ.
First John 2:1–2 directs believers who sin to Jesus Christ the righteous, our advocate with the Father, and speaks of His atoning sacrifice.
That is why the cross matters so deeply.
God does not save sinners by pretending sin does not matter.
He saves through the sacrifice of His Son.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than an answer to a theological question.
It becomes the difference between despair and hope.
Because some of you are carrying memories you have never told anyone.
A season of unbelief.
Words spoken in anger.
A deliberate act of rebellion.
A terrible thought you never wanted.
A private failure that still makes you feel ashamed.
And you have allowed those memories to become louder than the words of Christ.
You may be reading every biblical warning as though it were written exclusively to condemn you.
Every sermon becomes an accusation.
Every mention of judgment sends you searching your past.
Even prayer becomes frightening because you are afraid that God has stopped listening.
But please hear this distinction.
The Holy Spirit's conviction directs us toward truth, repentance, and Jesus Christ. Endless fearful speculation about whether mercy is impossible is not the same thing as biblical repentance.
If you are trapped in recurring fears about having committed this sin, you do not need to spend your life conducting a mental trial of every thought you have ever had.

You can speak with a wise pastor who handles Scripture carefully. If unwanted thoughts and repeated reassurance-seeking are consuming your daily life, support from a qualified mental-health professional can also help. Seeking that support does not mean your faith is deficient.
And above all, you can return to the actual words of Jesus rather than the worst interpretations your fear can imagine.
Because the invitation of the Gospel is not, “First prove that you are beyond all possible doubt.”
It is:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
There is a beautiful irony in Matthew 12 that deserves our attention.
The Pharisees were standing before the One who could forgive sins.
They witnessed evidence of His authority.
They heard His teaching.
Yet instead of receiving the truth, they attacked the source of His power.
And Jesus warned them.
That warning itself was a serious confrontation with their spiritual condition.
It exposed the danger of what they were saying.
And perhaps that is one of the most sobering realities in the entire passage.
You can be deeply religious and still resist the truth about Jesus.
You can know the language of Scripture and still misunderstand the heart of the Gospel.
You can defend your reputation for holiness while refusing to acknowledge God's work.
The Pharisees' problem was not a lack of religious activity.
It was their response to Christ.
And that should cause every one of us to examine ourselves.
Not merely the person who has fallen into obvious sin.
Not merely the skeptic.
Not merely the believer struggling with guilt.
All of us.
Because the question is not whether we can make ourselves look righteous in front of other people.
The question is whether we will humble ourselves before Jesus.
Will we receive His testimony?
Will we acknowledge our sin?
Will we surrender our pride?
Will we trust His mercy?
Will we follow Him even when obedience costs us something?
And will we stop confusing religious appearances with genuine faith?
There may be someone reading this who has never openly rejected Jesus but has spent years keeping Him at a safe distance.
You appreciate Christian messages.
You occasionally share Bible verses.
You believe that God exists.
But you have resisted surrender.
You want comfort without repentance.
You want forgiveness without acknowledging the seriousness of sin.
You want Jesus close enough to rescue you but not close enough to rule your life.
If that describes you, do not use the doctrine of grace as an excuse to remain unchanged.
Christ does not call us merely to admire Him.
He calls us to follow Him.
And His grace is not opposed to transformation.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Real grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes a new life possible.
And to the person who has been crushed by guilt, the same Gospel speaks with extraordinary tenderness.
You do not need to become your own savior.
You do not need to punish yourself until you feel worthy of forgiveness.
You do not need to replay your worst moment until you finally discover the perfect emotional response.
You need Christ.
The One who received Peter after his denial.
The One who showed mercy to Paul after his persecution.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners whom respectable society had written off.
The One who died for the ungodly.
The One who rose from the grave.
And the One who still calls people to repent and believe.
This is the heartbeat of what we mean at Gospel Warrior when we say:
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem a life that seemed hopelessly ruined.
He can take a person whose story is marked by shame and give that person a new identity in Him.
He can turn rebellion into repentance.
He can turn spiritual pride into humility.
He can turn a persecutor into a witness.
He can restore a fallen disciple.
And He can teach frightened believers to rest in the truth of His Word.
But the glory belongs to Jesus.
Not to the strength of our emotions.
Not to the beauty of our testimonies.
Not to a ministry, a writer, or a platform.
To Christ alone.
And that is why this message matters beyond the person reading it today.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list may be a person who has stopped attending church because they believe God no longer wants them.
Someone may be carrying shame from a season of rebellion.
Someone may be afraid of a thought they never chose to think.
Someone may be using religion to hide from the very Savior they need.
And someone may be dangerously comfortable with a hardened heart.
Not merely to increase the reach of a post.
But because someone you know may need to read Matthew 12 in its true context before another night of fear and misunderstanding.
And please, do not leave this conversation as though the subject is only theoretical.
Have you ever feared that you had sinned beyond God's forgiveness?
Have you ever misunderstood this passage?
Has Jesus brought you out of a season of rebellion, shame, or spiritual fear?
If you feel comfortable, share your testimony. You do not need to reveal private details.
And if this article has challenged you to stop hiding from God, you can write “no more hiding.”
Your honesty may encourage another believer who has been silently struggling with the same questions.
Not as a substitute for reading Scripture, but as a reminder to return to Matthew 12:22–32, Mark 3:22–30, John 6:37, and 1 John 1:9 whenever confusion about this warning arises.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, difficult questions are welcomed, repentance is never treated as unnecessary, and the grace of Jesus Christ is never forgotten.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into serious, Scripture-rooted discipleship.
And there is something personal I want to share with those who believe this work is worth sustaining.
Behind every carefully written article, every biblical resource, every effort to reach a wounded believer, and every attempt to explain difficult passages faithfully, there is ongoing work.
Time.
Research.
Preparation.
Resources.
And the desire to make Christ-centered teaching available to people who might never walk through the doors of a church.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
We invite you to support because you believe in the mission, value the resources, and want to help make them available to others.
Those products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, or tools for personal reflection.
It is helping more people hear about Jesus.
More Scripture explained.
More discipleship resources shared.
More difficult questions answered carefully.
More opportunities to point people away from despair and toward the Gospel.
Your presence is not measured by a payment.
The Gospel is not for sale.
It is proclaimed freely to sinners because of what Christ has accomplished.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought us here.
Can a Christian commit blasphemy against the Holy Spirit?
A professing Christian can certainly resist the Spirit, speak blasphemously, and harden their heart. A religious profession alone does not make someone incapable of serious spiritual rebellion.

But the New Testament also teaches that those who truly belong to Christ are kept by God's saving power, and Christians differ in how they explain perseverance, apostasy, and the application of this particular warning.
What we must not do is turn Matthew 12 into a claim that a genuine believer can accidentally lose salvation through an unwanted thought, a moment of fear, or an isolated sinful phrase.
That is not what the immediate passage describes.
Jesus was confronting people who were attributing the Spirit's work through Him to Satan.
The warning is severe because the rejection of God's testimony to Christ is severe.
It calls us to take unbelief seriously.
To resist spiritual hardness.
To repent rather than defend our sin.
And to recognize Jesus for who He truly is.
But if you are longing for Christ today, do not treat your longing as a reason to flee from Him.
Come to Him.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have been proud, humble yourself.
If you have been deceived, receive the truth of Scripture.
If you are afraid, listen to His promises.
If you are spiritually numb, do not make peace with that numbness. Ask God to awaken you to the truth.
And if you are unsure whether you have ever truly trusted Christ, do not build your hope upon a religious label.
Turn to the crucified and risen Savior in repentance and faith.
You can pray with words as simple as these:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned, and I cannot save myself. I do not want to hide behind excuses or live as though Your truth does not matter. Forgive me, cleanse me, and teach me to trust You. Deliver me from pride, unbelief, and the fear that keeps me from hearing Your Word clearly. Help me understand the Holy Spirit's testimony about You. Lead me into genuine repentance, living faith, and obedience. My hope is not in my ability to make myself worthy. My hope is in Your death and resurrection. Lord Jesus, have mercy on me. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magic formula.
The words themselves do not save.
Jesus Christ saves.
And the call of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Him.
So please remember this when the night becomes quiet and the old questions return.
Matthew 12 was never given so that you would ignore the danger of a hardened heart.
But neither was it given so that you would spend your life inventing reasons why the promises of Jesus cannot be trusted.
Read the warning.
Understand its context.
Take it seriously.
Then hear the Savior who said He would not cast out the one who comes to Him.
The final answer to your deepest spiritual need is not found in endlessly examining the darkness of your past.
It is found in the light of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the memory you have spent years using as proof that your story is over will become the very place where you finally learn to stop trusting your fear and start trusting the Savior.
